item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Majority of British adults approve of settlement ban, YouGov survey says
item.description:
Majority of British adults approve of settlement ban, YouGov survey says

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 09/10/2026 - 05:21
Green and Labour voters back the sanctions most strongly, with even Conservative approval narrowly outweighing disapproval
UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements and a ban on all arms licences and other exports that "materially contribute to the occupation". (AFP)
Off

A majority of British adults approve of the UK government’s decision to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, according to a YouGov survey.

The survey results released on Wednesday, and based on a poll conducted the same day among 4,506 UK adults, found that 52 percent of the adults approve of the ban, with 33 percent "completely” approving of the ban, while a further 19 percent "somewhat” approving it.

Ten percent of the surveyed adults said they "completely disapprove" and seven percent "somewhat disapprove" of the ban that has been backed by 11 other countries. Thirty-one percent of the respondents said they did not know.

A breakdown of the results by political affiliation shows 82 percent of Green Party supporters in favour of the ban: 59 percent “completely” and 23 percent “somewhat” approving, the highest of any political group in the country.

Labour party supporters also approved of the ban overwhelmingly, with 47 percent completely approving and 22 percent somewhat approving, for a total approval of 69 percent.

Only 17 percent of Conservative supporters completely approved and 21 percent somewhat approved, for 38 percent total approval, narrowly outweighing 34 percent total disapproval—12 percent somewhat disapproving and 22 percent completely. Twenty-seven percent voted ‘did not know’.

At 46 percent, Reform supporters expressed the highest disapproval of all the groups surveyed, with 31 percent saying they did not know.

Comprehensive sanctions

On Tuesday, the British government recognised the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, declared the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory illegal and announced both comprehensive sanctions on Israeli settlements and a ban on all arms licences and other exports that "materially contribute to the occupation".

Eleven other countries—Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden—signed a joint statement with Britain published on Tuesday, saying they "confirm their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements which are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and other measures, in accordance with their national procedures".

Israel reacted to the announcement by banning British MPs from entering the country. Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Israel would close the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem and remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center.

He further announced an end to British training of Palestinian forces and a ban on 11 British MPs from entering Israel.

The list includes former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, independent MP Zarah Sultana, Labour MPs Naz Shah, Diane Abbott, John McDonnell and Richard Burgon, and Green Party MPs Carla Denyer, Adrian Ramsay, Ellie Chowns, Sian Berry and Hannah Spencer.

In addition, Israel banned the lawyer Fahad Ansari, who has worked on a case arguing for Hamas to be de-proscribed as a terror organisation in Britain.

Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said on Tuesday afternoon: "I have visited all parts of Palestine on several occasions, where I have witnessed the horrors of occupation, as well as the resilience and humanity of the Palestinian people.

"They are the ones who suffer from Israel's apartheid. It is their freedom which is egregiously curtailed, alongside thousands of Palestinian refugees who are denied the right of return."

Corbyn added that "it is shocking that Israel continues to deny entry to UN investigators and international journalists. Israel doesn't want the world to see what it is doing - but we can never give up in our attempts to expose the truth".

Labour MP Naz Shah said the selection of MPs banned "appears rather random and, frankly, bizarre". 
She added: "I am proud to support the UK Government's actions today, taken in line with our international legal obligations."

'We will not be bullied into silence'

Labour MP Richard Burgon, a prominent campaigner in parliament for stronger action on Israel, said: "I’ve repeatedly called for sanctions on Israel over its war crimes and ethnic cleansing, including by providing evidence to the International Criminal Court.

"The decision by the Israeli government to sanction me today will not intimidate me into silence. I will continue to do what is right, speak out in defence of international law and stand up for justice for the Palestinian people."

All of the Green Party's MPs were banned by Israel. The Green Party has consistently called for sanctions on Israel, accused it of committing genocide in Gaza and backed the proscription of the Israeli military as a terrorist organisation.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "We will not be bullied into silence by the Israeli government. We are proud of our MPs for standing up for Palestinian rights and demanding an end to British complicity in genocide and illegal occupation.

"These threats only strengthen our resolve. The British government must stand firm and follow these overdue restrictions with a full arms embargo and wide-ranging sanctions."

Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party, added: "Our Green MPs have consistently spoken out and voted on the right side of history.

"Standing up against ethnic cleansing, occupation and genocide, as all MPs should be doing."
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in parliament on Tuesday afternoon that "the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful because of Israel's entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements".

This means the UK has accepted the 2024 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, which said the occupation is unlawful and placed a duty on states to oppose it.

Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists.

"And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this, and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] ‘I am trapped here’: Gulf-based Nepali workers agonise as devastating floods ravage home
item.description:
‘I am trapped here’: Gulf-based Nepali workers agonise as devastating floods ravage home

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Thu, 09/10/2026 - 06:24
Nepali workers in the Gulf are desperate to return home to help their loved ones but fear their employers will deny them leave or fire them from their jobs
People light candles on the national day of mourning in Kathmandu on 7 September to remember the thousands of Nepalis killed in the August flash floods (Prakash Mathema/AFP)
Off

Under Dubai’s blinding afternoon sun, Hari Krishna lays bricks for a luxury residential complex.

But his thoughts are 2,000 miles away, amid the mud and debris of Nepal’s Bhote Khosi-Trishuli corridor.

For the past week, the 32-year-old construction worker, who sends most of his earnings home, has spent every spare minute frantically trying to call his relatives on iMO and checking local news channels on his cracked smartphone.

Late August brought catastrophic flash floods to his home district of Nuwakot in Nepal. The waters swept away bridges, roads, and entire hillside settlements, leaving at least 1,399 people dead across the country and nearly 5,400 missing at the time of writing.

And like thousands of Nepalis, the floods swept away everything Krishna’s family owned - their house, household supplies, money, gold and a shed housing their cows and goats. With their land destroyed, Krishna said there is no possibility of farming in the future.

The disaster struck his hometown in the Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot District, claiming the life of his 67-year-old grandfather.

“I planned to visit my family for the upcoming Dashain festival, but that wish will now be unfulfilled with my grandfather gone,” Krishna told Middle East Eye, his voice trembling as he thought about the loss his family have experienced.

“My family is sleeping in a holding centre, terrified of the next landslide, and planning my grandfather’s final death rites.

“I asked my supervisor for emergency leave, but I don’t have the money for a sudden flight, and even if I did, the roads to my village are completely washed out.

“It would have been better if I was home and killed by the flood. I am trapped here.”

Krishna’s plight is echoed across the Gulf, where hundreds of thousands of Nepali migrants work to support their families back home. The glittering skylines of Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have been built largely by South Asian labour.

Now, as Nepal faces one of its most catastrophic climate disasters in recent history, the burden of rebuilding will inevitably fall on these same workers.

Nepal relies heavily on its diaspora, with remittances accounting for roughly a third of its gross domestic product; remittances from the Gulf, according to the Nepal Rastra Bank, account for 40 per cent of all Nepali remittances.

'A systematic horror'

UN agencies like the International Labour Organisation (ILO) note that extreme crises highlight how precarious the situation is for these workers.

Across the migration cycle, Nepali labourers face immense risks, from their wages being withheld to limited access to healthcare. 

Rameshwar Nepal, an investigator for Equidem, a global human and labour rights organisation, said many Nepali workers are desperate to leave but face overwhelming logistical hurdles.

“They are thousands of miles away [in the Gulf], while their families and communities face the devastation at home,” Nepal told MEE from Kathmandu, where he is coordinating relief efforts for workers and their families.

“They desperately want to return home and be with their families, see if they are still alive, and see the state of their homes, properties, relatives and communities for themselves.”

But the journey back is laced with fear and uncertainty about whether they can return to work in the Gulf.

“They don’t know whether they will be allowed to go, whether they will get paid leave, or, even if they are willing to go on unpaid leave, whether they will be allowed to do so,” Nepal explained.

Beyond securing permission and covering flight costs, workers fear the long-term impact on their livelihoods.

“Many of them need these jobs, particularly if they have lost their homes and property in the disaster. They need to know that they will still have a job to return to.”

Nepal pointed out that the region's labour sponsorship framework exacerbates this immobility, comparing the current anxiety to the Covid-19 lockdowns.

“The kafala system, which is a systematic kind of horror for migrant workers in terms of their freedom of mobility, is pertinent even in difficult situations like this,” he noted.

“We saw a similar situation back in 2020... They really wanted to return to their families, but they were prevented from doing so. It sounds like a very inhuman type of situation.”

'Starting from Zero' 

In Qatar, 37-year-old driver Shiva Ujjwal is living that exact nightmare.

Ujjwal has spent the last three years driving workers from the labour camps housing thousands of cleaners and construction workers on the outskirts of Doha to offices and building sites dotted across the Gulf capital.

The driver was starting his early morning shift when disaster struck. Without a chance to check social media, he first heard the news from fellow workers.

When his supervisor allowed him to use his phone, his frantic calls home failed - the communication networks in the region had been completely cut off.

“My heart was breaking,” Ujjwal said, recalling the first time he saw the devastating videos online.

“From the scale of the flood, I could easily imagine my house had been taken away, but I was very worried about my family.”

While his wife, children, and parents managed to escape safely, the human toll around them was staggering. Nine of his relatives were killed, and countless others from his village remain missing.

“My family members ran with empty hands, with no chance to take important papers, money, or gold,” he explained.

“We lost all our property in less than five seconds by a single hit of a live-bullet-type flood.”

Burden of rebuilding 

For Ujjwal, who previously worked in Saudi Arabia and the UAE before moving to Qatar three years ago, the material loss represents years of erased labour.

He had painstakingly built his family’s home in phases over several years, using his modest savings to fund one floor at a time. Though his Gulf wages were modest, the opportunity helped “light his kitchen” and keep his family afloat. Now, he faces the daunting prospect of starting from zero.

'We lost all our property in less than five seconds by a single hit of a live-bullet-type flood'

- Shiva Ujjwal, Nepalese worker in Qatar

His supervisor is arranging to send him back to Nepal on unpaid leave, but the geographic and emotional distance has taken a heavy toll, especially during the initial multi-day communication blackout.

“It is very stressful to stay here as my family is in a holding centre now,” he said, burdened by the thought of how to eventually rebuild their home. “My body is here, but I am not here.”

For the Nepali diaspora in the Gulf, the immediate response has been mobilisation. Grassroots fundraising campaigns are circulating through WhatsApp groups as workers pool their meagre savings to send bulk relief to the hardest-hit districts.

Yet, for men like Ujjwal and Krishna, the financial support feels like a hollow substitute for being home.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Democrats 'overwhelmingly' opposed to current Israeli regime, California governor says
item.description:
Democrats 'overwhelmingly' opposed to current Israeli regime, California governor says

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 09/10/2026 - 06:24
Gavin Newsom, a 2028 presidential hopeful, said the condemnation of what Bibi Netanyahu is doing is almost universal
Newsom said that everyone agrees Gaza has been a 'moral catastrophe'. (AFP)
Off

California Governor Gavin Newsom, a 2028 presidential hopeful, has said that Democratic Party was overwhelmingly opposed to the current Israeli regime and wanted a “secure democratic Palestinian state” right next door to a “democratic and secure” Israel.

In an interview with PBS News Hour’s Amna Nawaz, Newsom, who once called Israel an "apartheid state” and later retracted those comments, said: “It’s not even controversial anymore. The condemnation of what Bibi Netanyahu is doing is almost universal.” 

“There's not controversy within the party on that,” Newsom said, while acknowledging that “some of the language” by fellow Democrats “has been weaponised”. 

Newsom, one of the many American politicians who visited Israel in October 2023 and met families impacted by Hamas attacks, said certain “aspects of rhetoric” from individual candidates are on “the spectrum of concern”.

He said that the party is unified on the issue. “But I think universally, everyone agrees, even if you don’t think it’s genocide, that it’s been a moral catastrophe,” he said of the war in Gaza. 

“The vast majority of us also agree about the atrocities on 7 October and how horrific and unacceptable it was, and the terrorism that was perpetrated by Hamas.”

Referring to the ongoing settler violence in the occupied West Bank and Netanyahu’s opposition to a two-state solution, Newsom said: “We want a democratic and secure Israel, and we want a secure and democratic Palestinian state as well right next door. I don’t think that is a real divisive thing.” 

Newsom also told PBS News Hour that fewer Democrats were accepting donations from the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) lobby group.

“The vast majority of Democrats I talk to, even Democrats in the past that have in the past have taken AIPAC money, are pledging not to now,” Newsom added. 

“That’s more of a mainstream position, interestingly, within the Democratic Party.”

Diplomatic Isolation
Israeli opposition politicians have accused Netanyahu's government of driving the country into unprecedented global isolation after the United Kingdom announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid said the British decision to sanction settlements was "wrong", but turned his criticism on Netanyahu's government, accusing it of leading Israel "into unprecedented diplomatic isolation".

The government, he said, was "doing nothing but issuing rebukes and threats that no one takes seriously".

Gilad Kariv, a Knesset member from the left-wing Democrats party, also blamed Israel's far-right government for the sanctions, pointing to Israel's dispossession of Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank.

Kariv said the government was leading Israel into "international isolation," adding that Netanyahu had become politically "leprous" on the world stage.

"The citizens of Israel must not pay the price for his corrupt alliance with the nationalist fanatics," Kariv said on X, referring to Netanyahu's far-right coalition.

Michael Ben-Yair, a former Israeli attorney-general, went further, welcoming the British measures despite saying he did not welcome punitive action by one of Israel's allies.

Writing in the Financial Times, Ben-Yair said the measures were necessary to preserve the possibility of a political solution that could provide "peace and security for the seven million Jews and seven million Palestinians living between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River".

He argued that the measures distinguished between Israel's legitimacy as a state and its occupation of Palestinian territory, which he described as "morally, politically and legally unacceptable".

His comments came as Israel announced a series of retaliatory measures against Britain following Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's announcement of sanctions targeting settlement activity.

Miliband said the British government could no longer simply "call out" injustice and suffering, but had to act to oppose the expansion of Israeli settlements.

"Today we refuse to be bystanders to further suffering and to the destruction of the two-state solution," he said.

The measures were announced alongside a joint statement by 12 countries, including Britain, France, Canada, Spain, Denmark, Ireland, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, backing further restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] In Syria's Daraa, water is life - and today the land is parched
item.description:
In Syria's Daraa, water is life - and today the land is parched

Submitted by Mohammad Almasalma on Fri, 06/12/2026 - 20:22
Amid scarce rainfall, war-scarred infrastructure and the proliferation of unregulated wells, the region is in the grips of a severe water crisis
Off

Abdul-Munaf al-Masri stands before a vast, cracked expanse of land in southern Syria, where water once stretched to the horizon. 

Scattered stones and patches of dry grass cover what used to be Lake al-Muzayrib, while an abandoned boat rests on hardened soil - a remnant of another time. 

A few birds strut slowly across the empty basin, breaking the silence of a place that once teemed with life.

“I don’t like to come here,” Masri says quietly, his eyes fixed on the barren land. “The sight of drought saddens me.”

For more than two decades, Masri worked here as a fisherman. From 1993 until just a few years ago, Lake al-Muzayrib was not just a workplace, but the centre of his life.

That was until the lake northwest of Daraa city - once the province’s largest natural body of water, offering a vital resource for the local agricultural sector, and a means of survival for fishermen like Masri - began drying up. 

For years, researchers studying the Syrian war have been sounding the alarm about the water crisis gripping the country’s south. Prolonged periods of drought have been exacerbated by mismanagement of water resources, including excessive well-drilling in Daraa. 

Today, the region faces an unprecedented collapse in both surface and groundwater resources.

'I'm like a fish; if I leave this place, I die. The drought destroyed us'

- Abdul-Munaf al-Masri, resident

In the 1990s, the springs feeding Lake al-Muzayrib flowed at up to 1,000 litres per second; by 2016, that rate had fallen to less than 170 litres, and today, it is at zero, according to the Daraa Water Resources Directorate, a Syrian government agency.

The lake has dried up more than once in recent years, only to partially refill from rainfall - but by the end of 2024, it had entirely disappeared.

Masri’s eyes are sombre as he gazes across the parched lakebed. Forced to stop fishing here in 2021 after fish stocks collapsed, he has since scraped out a living by doing household jobs and plumbing. 

Masri is not alone in his predicament: around two dozen men used to fish these waters, but all have either left the country in recent years or had to find other work, he says.

“The lake means my life … I’m like a fish; if I leave this place, I die,” Masri tells Middle East Eye. “The drought destroyed us. I was born and raised here, and it’s hard for a person to lose something so precious.”

Resources dwindling

For millennia, life in southern Syria has unfolded in close relation to the surrounding environment. 

The region’s rich volcanic soil and abundant water resources, particularly in the Hauran plains, have enabled generations of Syrians to live off the fertile land, cultivating grains, vegetables and livestock.

Encompassing Quneitra, Daraa and Suwayda provinces, which meet at the borders of Jordan and historic Palestine, the region’s position as a strategic crossroads has also contributed to its geographic and economic value. 

But in recent years, the water crisis has come to dominate the local landscape: out of 16 dams in Daraa, 14 have experienced partial or total drying, according to engineer Hani al-Abdullah, the province’s director of water resources.

Once a popular tourist destination known for its lush banks and scenic beauty, Lake al-Muzayrib is symptomatic of this larger trend of decline, which has also seen several key feeder springs dry up or slow to a trickle. 

According to the Daraa water directorate, the total storage capacity across the province’s 16 dams is 92.5 million cubic metres, but despite significant year-on-year variations due to rainfall, it now holds only a tiny fraction of that. In 2025, the total amount stored was less than four million cubic metres - the lowest level recorded this century, and a huge drop from 65 million cubic metres just five years earlier.

The critical water situation threatens all aspects of life in the province, with Abdullah citing a continuous decline in this vital resource over the past several decades. He speaks to MEE from the crest of the Daraa Dam, a massive reservoir that today is almost completely dry.

For many years, this dam was a popular destination for local residents, known for its abundance of fish and its crucial role in irrigating surrounding farmland. The scene now is strikingly different: the water has largely receded, and trees have been cut down across the barren landscape. 

The dam once echoed with birdsong and the voices of children at play. Today, there is only silence.

Farmers in jeopardy

For many families across Daraa, agriculture is a livelihood passed down through generations. It forms the backbone of the local economy, in a region known for its rich production of tomatoes, olives, pomegranates and grapes, among other produce.

War has ravaged this economy. During more than 14 years of open conflict between government forces and Syrian rebels, farmers watched helplessly as water and irrigation networks were targeted, and trade links cut off.

In the town of Tafas, in the western countryside of Daraa, Abu Mahmoud speaks with quiet frustration as he scrolls through comments on social media blaming farmers for the depletion of freshwater springs used for drinking.

“I own five dunams [0.5 hectares] of land planted with pomegranates,” he tells MEE. “It has always been my family’s main source of income. But in recent years, everything has changed - the war, the drought … nothing is the same anymore.”

Like thousands of other Syrians, Abu Mahmoud, who spoke under a pseudonym for fear of repercussions, found himself breaking the law to survive. Amid a vacuum of governmental authority during the war, he dug an unlicensed well in a desperate attempt to save his crops.

“I had no choice,” he says. “We all did the same. It was the only way to keep working and protect our land. But even that wasn’t a real solution. It cost a lot, and after three years, the well dried up.”

Abu Mahmoud dug the well in 2015, at a time when the collapse of state oversight had led to a surge in unregulated drilling across the region. Thousands of illegal wells have since appeared across western Daraa, according to local authorities - transforming what was once a temporary solution into a widespread phenomenon.

Today, residents increasingly blame these wells for the region’s worsening water shortages.

Water itself has been transformed into a costly commodity, placing a heavy burden on families: the price of 1,000 litres of water has risen in recent years to around $5, an amount that is difficult to afford for many people, in a region where the average monthly salary is roughly between $75 and $150.

Abdullah says his directorate has received dozens of complaints about illegal wells, with residents linking them to the drying up of natural springs and the disruption of drinking water supplies. He says authorities have taken steps to combat the problem - ramping up monitoring efforts, repairing damaged irrigation networks, drilling regulated wells in areas facing shortages, and trucking in water from neighbouring areas - in an effort to further deter unregulated groundwater extraction.

Dozens of drilling rigs have also been confiscated, after the governor of Daraa last year issued a decision mandating the seizure of equipment used to construct illegal wells, alongside fines for those who build them - but the problem has become so widespread that it is difficult to control.

'A well is not a luxury. It's a lifeline - not just for me, but for dozens of families in this town'

- Hatem al-Zoubi, farmer

The same reality unfolds in eastern Daraa, where Hatem al-Zoubi walks slowly across his land, carrying a sickle and an axe. He pauses among rows of olive trees, which he tends with care, as if they were members of his own family. 

His land sustains 700 olive trees, while he cultivates legumes, citrus fruits and tomatoes across 20 dunams (two hectares). On the corner of Zoubi’s farm, next to a concrete fence by his vineyard, stands a well he dug in 2020.

“A well is not a luxury,” Zoubi tells MEE. “It’s a lifeline - not just for me, but for dozens of families in this town.”

Beyond irrigation for farmland, the well on his land supplies drinking water to many residents, he says, noting that its closure would cut off a vital community resource.

“Without it, the town would have faced real drinking water crises, especially in the summer,” he says. “This year, with more displaced people and livestock, the need for water has only grown.”

High costs, limited returns

For farmers like Zoubi, wells are both a necessity and a burden - a fragile lifeline in a region where water, once abundant, is becoming increasingly scarce.

Drilling and equipping the well, which depends on solar energy, cost him around $70,000, Zoubi says. Returns are barely covering those expenses, amid low prices for agricultural products and increasing costs for fertilizers and pesticides, alongside frequent technical failures, which can run to thousands of dollars in repairs and losses. 

In the area of Lake al-Muzayrib alone, Masri estimates that there are more than 7,000 illegal wells, leading to severe groundwater depletion.

“People don’t realise the danger … Someone may dig a well to water their own trees, but in doing so, they destroy an entire community,” he says.

Abdullah, Daraa’s director of water resources, confirms that local groundwater levels have dropped significantly, by five to 10 metres in some areas, due to excessive pumping and increased demand. The use of solar energy to operate wells has further accelerated extraction rates, worsening depletion.

In western Daraa, student Basel al-Zoubi, who lived as a refugee in Jordan until the fall of the Assad regime, recently returned to the small town of Tseel, where many people now rely on purchasing water delivered by tankers to meet their daily needs.

Zoubi tells MEE that the town urgently need pumping systems capable of transporting water from springs and state-managed wells to residential areas, after much of the existing infrastructure was damaged in the war.

The impact of war on Syrian water is so vast, you can see it from space
Kieran Cooke
Read More »

Walking through the streets of Tseel, the destruction is still visible in the crumbling storefronts and ruined roadways, while the hum of generators fills the air. 

“Water is a lifeline,” Zoubi says. “There is no alternative, especially given the difficult economic conditions people are facing.”

Along with rehabilitating and repairing the water network to ensure consistent access for residents, Zoubi believes the government should impose a stricter system for regulating wells, “and those that encroach on drinking water sources should be shut down” more swiftly.

Masri also calls for tighter regulation around wells, a campaign to raise community awareness, and the establishment of a fisherman’s union that could focus on restocking dams if water levels recover.

But efforts by water authorities in Daraa to tackle the problem remain limited in scope, underscoring the need for a comprehensive strategy that balances water conservation with sustaining livelihoods in a region where water has become synonymous with survival.

Amin al-Haibi, a fisherman from Daraa, confirms that drought has “destroyed our profession”. Only al-Wehda Dam, located on the Yarmouk River at the Jordanian border, remains as a limited source of local fishing, highlighting the near-total collapse of this sector.

Masri’s face fills with sorrow as he recalls the abundance of the past. 

“Sometimes we used to catch 200 or 300 kilograms a day,” he recalls, noting that the bountiful waters allowed him to support his family with ease. “It made you happy.” 

Today, that reality has vanished with the water; the boats that once fed around 100 families turned into scrap.

“Nothing encourages me to come here anymore. The drought, the cutting of trees - it’s painful,” Masri says. 

“We hope life returns as it was before.”

item.description:

Labor introducing new laws to crack down on illegal tobacco

Labor will introduce new laws to make it easier to prosecute criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade, as the government fights an uphill battle against the exploding black market.

The new laws think about it as a list of observable indicators, very simple, fact-based things like: is the tobacco appropriately packaged? Is it a menthol cigarette even hiding in plain packaging? Is it being concealed? Does it have paperwork at the border?

Or my personal favourite: is the retail price of this packet of cigarettes less than the amount of excise and GST combined? If any of these facts are proven, just one of them, that establishes the reasonable suspicion of the criminal offence of importing, possession, or conveying. It’ll give powerful new tools to Border Force but every state and territory police force to go after the crooks.
